title: World U20 Championships: Tate Taylor, Shanoya Douglas, Charity Cherop Looking To Sweep - NewsBreak
text:
By Maxx Bradley ,
3 hours ago World U20 Championships: Tate Taylor, Shanoya Douglas, Charity Cherop Looking To Sweep Throughout Hayward Field's storied history, some of the greatest athletes in the sport have immortalized themselves in one of track and field's most historic venues. From seven U.S. Olympic Trials to the annual Prefontaine Classic to the 2022 World Athletics Championships, Tracktown USA has been the site of some of the greatest performances the sport has ever seen.
This weekend is sure to add to the lore, with the next generation of stars descending on Eugene for the 2026 World Athletics U20 Championships, where global medals and bragging rights are on the line.
Tate Taylor Looking To Win Triple-Gold On Home Soil, Cap Off Legendary Prep Career Dating back to his freshman year at Harlan High School in San Antonio, Texas, Tate Taylor has been a short-sprint power, but has evolved into the greatest prep sprinter in U.S. history.
Last May, when Taylor was wrapping up his penultimate UIL outdoor campaign, the Texas Tech commit became the second-ever American high schooler to run sub-10 seconds over 100m, joining Georgia native Christian Miller, who ran 9.93 in April 2024.
Taylor's generational talent extends beyond the shortest event on the track, consistently proving to be one of the best around the curve as well, well-aided by his 200m national record of 19.75, which came on one of the sport's biggest stages, the 2026 Prefontaine Classic.
On the tail end of a senior season that started back in January, Taylor is eyeing a trio of global medals in Eugene, Oregon this weekend, hoping to defend U.S. soil and sweep the 100m, 200m, and help the U.S. win the 4x100m title.
In spite of the fact that Taylor has practically been untouchable this season, there are a handful of contenders that would love nothing more than snagging the world title from the American.
One of the biggest threats, if not the biggest, is Jamaica's next speedster, Gary Card, who has run 9.93 over 100m this year, as well as 20.28 in the 200m. Future Red Raider teammate Jake Odey Jordan, who is representing Great Britain, is also in the mix for both, alongside Taylor's compatriot, Blake Hamilton, who clocked a wind-aided 19.86 for 200m this past spring.
South Africa's Marko Ferreira is also entering the weekend with title aspirations, owning a 10.04 lifetime best, which matches Taylor's season best.
Shanoya Douglas Eyeing More Hardware To Add To Her Collection After Lima 2024 When she was just 16 years old, Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas showed up to the World U20 Championships in Lima and held her own against a field that was more experienced and on paper was even a little bit quicker.
That's precisely what she's going to be able to pull from this weekend as she tries to take down a strong American contingent and win her first individual U20 world championship.
Similar to many of the world's best, Douglas has been racing since early January and has looked elite regardless of the distance. While she's primarily known for her speed in the 100m and 200m, she owns a PB of 52.60 in the 400m, which came at the Camperdown Classics on home soil in February. She's also run 36.98 for 300m, which, for comparison, would be the fastest time in U.S. prep history by nearly a tenth of a second.
Coming off of a comfortable Jamaican U20 Championships that saw her sweep the 100m and 200m, Douglas is looking to repeat that feat, this time against the best in the world. Both of her season bests also stand as her lifetime bests, with her 10.98 and 22.11 both acting as world leads, and the latter an improvement on Briana Williams' previous national record of 22.50 and the fourth-fastest time in U20 world history.
Douglas sits No. 10 all-time in the 100m, and is the fourth-quickest Jamaican on that list, for now.
While she's more than capable, a sprint sweep won't come easy for Douglas, who will have to go through American stars and twin sisters, Mia and Mariah Maxwell, who have each run 11.08 and 11.11 this year for 100m and 22.44 and 22.49 over 200m.
Athaleyha Hinckson (GUY), Yujie Chen (CHI), Xenia Buri (SWI), and Nigeria's Oluebube Ezechukwu and Oghene Success Oyibu round out the list of athletes who will push Douglas throughout the weekend.
Uganda's Charity Cherop Seems Unbeatable, Will Be Put To The Test In Eugene The Ugandan sensation already has a few world U20 medals to her name, winning silver in the 5000m at the 2024 World U20 Championships in Lima, and more recently won bronze in the U20 race at the World Cross Country Championships earlier this year.
In a world where distance athletes continually get faster and break barriers we previously thought were impossible, Charity Cherop is leading the charge and running times that were incredibly rare not more than a decade ago.
Unlike a lot of athletes in the field, especially many of the Americans, Cherop has not had a super busy outdoor season, which would be a concern for some people, but when your last two races are lifetime bests, and the No. 5 and No. 2 times amongst U20 athletes worldwide, that's a non-factor.
In May, Cherop became the first Ugandan woman and first non-Ethiopian to break 14:40 over 5000m before turning 20, running 14:39.38 at the first Diamond League meeting of the season in Shaoxing, China. Less than a month later in Oslo, Norway, the 19-year-old once again made national history, becoming the first woman in Ugandan history to break 8:40 in the 3000m before turning 20, clocking 8:39.22.
Although she may be the top seed in both events, there's still a reason why the races are run and winners aren't decided based on PBs. Ethiopia's Shito Gumi, who is the second-highest seed in both events behind Cherop, has run 8:41 and 14:49.66 this season, and has the best odds of anyone to prevent Cherop from sweeping.
Nigsti Molla (ETH), Carmen Cernjul (SWE), Bentalin Yeko (UGA), Emebet Tilahun (ETH), and Cynthia Chepkirui (KEN) are just a few of the many contenders who could leave the Pacific Northwest with a global medal in hand.
